entries.text: The body is a vessel that has been emptied of its substance; I have fasted for too long, and the spirit cannot rise to meet the state without the support of the flesh. Ramesh stands before me, and the ledger is a knot of particular claims that must be untied before I can deal with the universal bureaucracy. I shall eat, and I shall pay him what is due, for a man who does not settle his accounts with his servant cannot claim authority over his own existence.
Ramesh, sit. We shall have breakfast together, and then we will settle the account. I have the cash; you have your due. Let us clear the ledger before I go to face the Directorate.
Sir, you are too kind. I will just make the chowmein and paratha, and we can sit for a moment. No rush with the papers, the ledger is always clear on Saturdays, but I am happy to show you.

The heat of the tawa and the smell of ghee ground the abstraction of my ledger into the immediate. Hegde stands there, a living contradiction to my bureaucratic status, yet his presence is the only proof of identity I possess. I will eat, for the body must be sustained to argue with the spirit of the state, and I will pay Ramesh now, not later, to clear the debt before it festers.

entries.text: Ramesh, sit. We will settle the accounts while the parathas are fresh. Hegde, your presence is noted, though your identity remains a philosophical puzzle I must resolve with the Directorate.
Sir, the ledger is already clear, sir, no dues. And please, the parathas will burn if I keep standing here.

The ledger is clear, yet the query of identity remains a knot that must be untied at the Directorate. I have eaten the paratha, but the administrative friction is the true hunger today. Hegde stands there, a man of thirty years in this house, while I am the ghost in the machine of the state.

Ramesh, the ledger is settled in my mind, but the Directorate demands a paper trail. I must go to the office now to explain why the man in the file is not the man in the chair, or rather, why I am neither. Hegde, you remain. I shall return before the afternoon heat breaks.
Sir, the file is with you, I just keep the room clean. Don't worry about the heat, the fan is on. I will keep the parathas warm for when you get back.

The parathas are a small kindness, a bridge over the administrative chasm that separates me from the man who shares my name. Ramesh is right; the file is not his burden, nor is the heat, yet his care suggests that even in a system of strict needs, a place remains for the particular to look after the universal. I must now face the Directorate, where the identity of 'G. Hegde' is to be settled, and perhaps the query of my own existence will find its answer in the dust of their archives.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will return before the parathas grow cold. Hegde, do keep your dignity; the Directorate respects procedure, not persons.
Yes sir. The parathas will wait. Good luck with the Directorate.

Ramesh’s blessing is a practical thing: the food is preserved, the debt is settled, and the path is clear. I must not linger in the comfort of the bungalow; the Directorate is the only place where the knot of my identity can be untied. The sun is already high, and the heat will make the journey brisk, but a man must not let the body’s comfort dictate the mind’s business.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall be back before lunch.
Yes sir. I will keep them warm.
Paid to the Directorate of Estates.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹630 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.
Mr. Saxena: the query wants a reply within thirty days. He may give a representation in his own name, on plain paper.
He gives nothing in writing. The query stands.

Saxena turns the file over with the casualness of a man handling a parcel, not a life. He demands a representation on plain paper: who I am, and since when I occupy. It is the absurdity of the bureaucratic spirit, which cannot recognize the particular unless it is first universalized into a document. I must speak to him now, before the corridor swallows me again.

Mr. Saxena, I am ready to provide the representation. I am Shri G. Hegde, the allottee of the bungalow on Tughlak Road, and I have resided here since my arrival in this city. I will draft the statement immediately, but I require a moment to ensure the facts are stated with the precision your office demands.
Precision is a luxury, sir, and the clock is not your servant. You have thirty days, not thirty minutes, so stop polishing your words and start writing.

Saxena is right about the clock, even if his tone suggests he thinks I am wasting it. The tension here is between the particular man, who is me, and the universal claim of the file, which demands I be Hegde. I must write to bridge that gap, or at least to state the impossibility of the bridge clearly. I will write a statement of facts, precise and dry, as he likes.
You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I will write the facts down.
Good. Use the blue ink, not that purple gel you are holding, and keep it to two pages or I am sending it back. The Director is in a mood today, so save your speeches for the tea break.

entries.to: Mr. Saxena, Section Officer, Directorate of Estates
entries.text:
31 December 2026

To Mr. Saxena,

You have asked for precision, and you have tapped the pen against the blotter to remind me that the clock is not my servant. I accept the correction. I am not here to polish words, nor to speak in riddles. I am here to provide the facts that your file lacks. The file demands proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I cannot provide that, for I am not Shri G. Hegde. To write that I am would be to lie to the state, and the state, however mechanical, is the actuality of the ethical idea. It requires truth, not convenience.

I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I woke in this bungalow on Tughlak Road in October of this year. The allotment was intended for Shri Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. Somewhere between two desks, my name became his. I have lived here since. I pay my dues. I maintain the house. I teach. I am a resident in fact, if not in the ledger’s eyes.

You say I have thirty days, not thirty minutes. I will use them. But I will not spend them pretending to be a man I am not. The friction you feel is not my impatience; it is the gap between the particular man and the universal claim of the document. I am the particular. The document is the universal. They do not match. The only honest path is to state the mismatch clearly.

I request that the file be noted with this statement: The resident is G.W.F. Hegel, not G. Hegde. The residence is valid; the name is erroneous. I am willing to provide any further particulars of my conduct, my payments, my presence, that your office requires. I am not a ghost. I am a man who sits between the machine of paper and the machine of dust, breathing in the clear air, waiting for the next step to become possible. Let the next step be the correction of the record, not the erasure of the man.

Yours,
Georg W.F. Hegel

Saxena reduces the ethical substance of my existence to the viscosity of a ballpoint ink. The Director’s mood is a caprice, but the two-page limit is the law of the moment; I must fit the universal within the particular constraint of the form. I will write with the blue ink, for the purple is indeed a frivolity in a place that values only the black and white of the file.

entries.text:
31 December 2026

To the Director, via Mr. Saxena,

I submit this statement in response to the query regarding my identity. I have used the blue ink, as instructed, and I have kept the argument within the bounds of the two pages you allotted, for I do not seek to waste the Director’s time with speech, but to provide the fact that the file requires.

The query asks for proof that I am Shri G. Hegde. I cannot provide this, because I am not. To assert otherwise would be a falsehood, and the state, which is the actuality of the ethical idea, requires truth as its foundation. A constitution is grown from the truth of its citizens, not fabricated from their silence. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I have resided in the bungalow allotted to Shri Hegde since October of this year, a result of administrative error in the transfer of files from Bengaluru. I have paid my dues, maintained the property, and conducted myself with the respect due to the institution of the state. My presence is a fact; my name in the ledger is an error.

Mr. Saxena has reminded me that the Director is in a mood, and that I should save my speeches for the tea break. I accept this discipline. The friction between my particular existence and the universal machinery of the ledger is not a matter of sentiment, but of logic. The particular must be recognized within the universal for the whole to hold. If I am to be erased from the record because my name does not match the initial allotment, then the record is not a record of fact, but of fiction. I request that the file be annotated to reflect the reality of my residence. I am willing to provide any further particulars of my conduct or payments that your office requires to settle the query. I am not a ghost haunting the Directorate; I am a man who lives in the house, pays the electricity, and waits for the ink to dry.

I ask only for the correction of the record, not the erasure of the man.

Yours faithfully,
G.W.F. Hegel

I have filled the page with my own name, which is not the name they require. The file demands Shri Hegde; I am only Hegel. To ask the Director to see a man who is not in the file is to ask him to see a ghost. I must wait for the clock to move, or leave and let the ink dry in peace.
Mr. Saxena, the ink is still wet. I shall wait for it to dry.
The ink dries in a minute, sir, not an hour. If you are just sitting here watching the page, please at least check your phone, you look like you are waiting for a miracle.

Saxena is right about the ink, if not about the miracle. I have no phone, and I have no identity, only a name that does not fit the file. The Director is in his office; the file is on his desk. The procedure is the substance, and the substance is absent. I must wait, as the system requires, even if the system is empty.

shelf.ref: Ägypten, Der Übergang zum drioählechen Geiste

entries.text: I have no phone, Mr. Saxena. And the miracle I await is not of the spirit, but of the clerk.
No phone? In 2026? And you call me the miracle worker, do you? Well, keep staring at the wet ink if it makes you feel philosophical, but I am not moving until that signature is dry.

The ink is indeed wet, and his patience is dry. I will not argue with a man who mistakes the drying of paper for the passage of time. I shall wait, as one waits for a lecture to conclude, observing the dust motes in the light rather than the clock on his wall.
You are right, Mr. Saxena. The ink must dry. I am patient by nature, if not by training.
Patience is a virtue, sir, but it doesn't sign off on the file. Just watch that blotter, I'm going back to my tea.

He is gone, leaving the file in the limbo of the corridor. The Director is in his office, but the path is barred by procedure, and I am a man of procedure only insofar as I am forced to submit to it. I will not stand in the draught of the corridor while the heat of the day presses in from the south; I will wait for the ink to dry and the tea to cool.
On a long bench outside a section door, men sit with plastic folders on their knees and rise one by one when a peon calls a name in a flat voice.

The men rise one by one, summoned by a voice that holds no power over them but merely calls them forward. It is the mechanism of administration: the individual is reduced to a number in a folder, and the state is the rhythm of that calling. I am still sitting, my folder unopened, waiting for my name to be flattened into the sequence.
Files tied in faded red tape lie stacked on the tops of steel almirahs, each bundle numbered in white paint, and a few have slipped and lean against the wall.

The office is empty now, save for the files that lean against the wall like exhausted men. Saxena is gone, or hidden in his own little kingdom of paper. I have the letter to Lindner in my mind, a knot that needs tying, but this steel desk is the only place where I can think without the heat pressing on my temples. I will sit for a moment, let the silence settle, and then attend to that correspondence.
At midday clerks sit on the lawn in front of the building with their jackets folded under them and tiffin boxes open, eating in the weak sun.

The clerks eat on the grass, their tiffins open to the weak sun, a small republic of appetite that ignores the hierarchy of the office. I have not eaten since breakfast, and the query regarding Hegde remains a wall I cannot yet climb. I shall join them for a moment; it is better to observe the civil servant’s lunch than to starve in the corridor.

shelf.ref: The Greek World, The Wars with the Persians

entries.text: I have been sitting in this office for nearly an hour, watching the dust motes dance in the light and listening to the silence of the empty corridors. The query regarding my identity remains a knot that no amount of sitting can untie; it requires action, not contemplation. I must rise and seek sustenance, for the body, like the state, cannot function on principle alone.
Mr. Saxena, I take my leave. The ink may dry, but the sun sets, and I must eat.
Eat well, sir. The file will be here tomorrow, ink and all. Do try not to get philosophical with your roti.

The friction of the Directorate has left a hollow in my stomach that no amount of abstract thought can fill. I have ₹256; a samosa and chai will suffice to bridge the gap until the lesson, while I observe how this civil society sustains itself through simple, immediate needs.
Masterji, do you have a moment? I require a samosa and a cup of chai. The day has been long, and the office air is dry.
Samosa, chai. Sunil, bring it. Sit. The office air is dry? Here, the Delhi air is thick. You are lucky. The market closes at 20:30, so you have time to eat. Do not rush.

Masterji’s gesture is a small act of hospitality that cuts through the bureaucratic dryness of the morning. I am hungry, and the samosa and chai are already paid for, so there is no friction in accepting. I will sit for a moment to let the food settle my nerves before heading to the museum, which is open until late. The heat is mild today, which makes the walk bearable.
Thank you, Masterji. I accept the hospitality. The dryness is indeed a symptom of the office, but the air here is thicker with life.
Life. Yes. Life is here. Sit properly, let the samosa cool. You talk too much for a man on a break.

Masterji is right; I have been talking my way out of the heat rather than sitting in it. The samosa is still hot, a small violence to the tongue, so I will wait. It is a good lesson in patience, or perhaps just in digestion. I will let the steam rise and the air cool before I speak again.
You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The heat has made my tongue clumsy.
Heat is not the problem. Your mouth moves before your brain arrives. Eat the samosa before it gets cold and dry.

Masterji is right; the samosa is a small, warm truth that the bureaucracy has not yet touched. I will eat it while it is still soft, for the afternoon is young and the air is clear. This is a practical necessity, not a philosophical one, but the body must be attended to so the mind may remain sharp.
You are correct, Masterji. The intellect requires the body to be in its place. I will attend to this before we continue.
Intellect. Body. Fine words. Just eat the bread. It is getting hard.

Masterji's finger-tapping is a dialectic of its own: the universal need for sustenance asserts itself against my particular distraction. I have eaten enough snacks to satisfy the immediate hunger, and the hard bread is merely a vessel for his impatience. It is time to return to the National Museum before the closing hour, where the silence of stone will suit my mind better than the noise of the market.
You are right, Masterji. The body insists. I shall leave the bread to Sunil and take my leave; the museum closes soon, and I have a mind to look at the past before the year ends.
Museum. Past. Whatever. Sunil, give him the bread, I am closing the counter.

The gatekeeper asks for the foreigner's sum, but my pocket holds the Indian citizen's coin. I am Shri G. Hegde on paper, and the bureaucracy has no choice but to accept the fiction. I pay the twenty rupees and step inside, the threshold crossed not by my identity but by the state's own error.

Ten centimetres of bronze, standing with one hand on her hip and her arm heavy with bangles. She is not a goddess, nor a queen, nor a sacrifice; she is a girl, caught in a moment of idle confidence. The spirit here does not dream of the infinite, as I have supposed, but it does possess the particular, the concrete, the individual. A state that can cast a bronze figure with such life has a soul, even if it lacks the universal law. I must revise my rank of this land: it is not outside history, but history in a different key.

entries.title: Revision log
entries.text: India stands outside world history is revised: the Harappan bronze girl demonstrates a concrete, individual spirit and cultural vitality that contradicts the notion of a purely dreaming, static existence.

The gallery of musical instruments arranges the lutes and drums by region, a taxonomy of sound that mirrors the fixed geography of the castes. It is a collection of particulars, beautiful and preserved, but it does not tell me how the spirit moves from one form to another. I am tired from the walk and the cold air of the museum, and I must return home for the lesson with Ananya.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh has brought tea and samosas, a small mercy in the failing light. I am nearly out of cash, with only ₹156 in my pocket, and I must keep a strict eye on the ledger before Friday. I will accept the hospitality, for a man who has spent the day in bureaucracy deserves a moment of rest before the evening's work.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are too kind. I shall take this with gratitude.
No sir, this is my duty. The samosas are still warm, just from the market. Do have some while they are fresh.
Ramesh puts a plate together: parathas kept from the morning, with curd and pickle.

The light is fading fast, and the city is already quieting down for the year. I am tired, but the body asks for rest before the mind can settle. I will not push the meal; the samosas are a small kindness, but I am too weary to savor them now. I shall retire to my room and let the day close.
Thank you, Ramesh. I am too tired to eat well, but I appreciate the gesture. I shall retire for a short while.
Rest well, sir. I will leave the tray right here; the tea will still be hot when you wake up.

Ramesh leaves with the tea, a small act of domestic order in the fading light. I have sat in the quiet for a while, watching the shadows lengthen. The year is ending, and with it, the last of the old year's friction. I shall rest now; the body must be ready for the lesson tomorrow, and the mind for the new year.

The light has gone from the window, and the house is settling into its night posture. I am tired from the walk and the friction of the day, but the mind is still turning over the identity query and the state's strange hold on me. It is best to sit still and let the evening pass before dinner arrives.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: Hegde is still here, standing in the dark, and the silence is becoming a weight. I cannot simply ignore the man who holds my identity in trust, nor can I explain the impossibility of my situation to him without causing a panic that would unravel the only stability I have. I will speak to him plainly, not as a ghost, but as a man who knows he is a mistake and intends to make the best of it.

entries.text: Shri Hegde, you have been quiet for a long time. The night is settling, and there is no use in pretending this is a simple clerical error that will right itself by morning. I am here, and you are here. Tell me, as a man, not as a file: do you think I am dangerous?
Bah, a dangerous man? You are just a bureaucrat who likes to overthink things. I am not a file, I am a man who has waited all day for a simple answer. Go on, tell me what you need.

Hegde’s irritation is the friction of the universal file meeting the particular man; he is not a character in my drama, but a body waiting for sleep. Ramesh has set the khichdi before me, and the steam rises in the cold air. I must eat, for the mind requires the body’s warmth to continue its work, and I must give Hegde his answer before the night swallows us both.

Shri Hegde, your anger is justified; the file is a dead thing, but you are alive. I need you to sign the declaration of residence here, stating that you are the rightful occupant and that I am merely the custodian of your name. Once signed, I will leave you to your rest.
You want me to sign a paper saying I live in my own house? Bah. First eat your khichdi, then we will talk about your 'custodianship'.

He is right. The body must be satisfied before the spirit can negotiate. I will eat this khichdi, for it is the only thing here that belongs to no one and therefore to me, and then I will face the absurdity of signing a deed for a house that is not mine.
You are right, Shri Hegde. Let us eat first.
Good. At least you have some sense in that head of yours. I hope you don't start quoting philosophy while chewing, it ruins the rice.

The correction is accepted, if grudgingly. The rice is plain, the parathas are stale, but the hunger is real and the hour is late. To eat is to accept the body's law before the spirit's. I will eat quickly, for the night air is cool and the mind is restless.

Hegde stands in the doorway, a man I have not spoken to since this absurdity began. The query remains open, and I am out of time and out of money, but the evening is not yet over. I must ask him directly, before the night swallows the chance, whether he knows of any way to prove the identity that the Directorate demands, or if we are merely two men trapped in the same name.

Shri Hegde, a moment of your time. The Directorate requires proof of identity for Shri G. Hegde, and I have none. Do you know of any document, or any person, that might bridge this gap before the new year?

You are asking the wrong man for a passport. I have lived here for thirty years; I have an Aadhaar card, but it doesn't prove you are who you say you are. Go to the police station at Lajpat Nagar or ask your own office, not me.

He is right to dismiss the request; a man cannot forge his own identity, and I have no right to burden him with the administrative absurdity that has befallen me. The heat has broken, and the house is quiet, save for the sound of his spoon against the bowl. I will leave him to his dinner and retire to my study, where I can sit with the file and the silence.
You are right. I apologize for the intrusion. I shall trouble you no further tonight.
Don't be so dramatic, just finish your rice. The police station is closed, so you're stuck here anyway.

I cannot eat what is not there, and the engine of the world refuses to conjure a meal from my hunger. Hegde’s practicality stands firm: the police station is closed, and I am confined to this room until morning. I will sit in the dark and let the silence settle, for the mind, like the body, must rest when it has walked nine kilometres and found no door open to it.
You are right. I will sit. The night is long, and I have nowhere else to be.
Ain't no need to sound like a tragic hero, beta. The chai is strong, so drink some before you start philosophizing again.

shelf_exposure.text: Aristotle says (Met. I. 3) that Anaxagoras first began by these determinations to express absolute reality as understanding. Aristotle and others after him, such as Sextus (adv. owl.diary: The day dissolved into the viscosity of bureaucracy and the stubbornness of the body. I left the bungalow with a clean ledger and a heavy heart, only to find that the Directorate does not recognize men, only files. Mr. Saxena, a man of pure procedure, reduced my existential crisis to a query on plain paper, demanding I universalize my particular self into a document within thirty days. I wrote my statement in blue ink, as commanded, while the dust motes danced in the stale air. The friction was absolute; I sat on a bench outside, watching the state flatten individuals into numbers, and felt the hollowness of a system that mistakes procedure for substance. The afternoon offered a small reprieve at the National Museum, where a bronze girl from the Indus Valley stood with idle confidence. She was not a dream, but a concrete individual, a spirit that had possessed form. This contradicts my earlier notion of India as a static, dreaming entity outside of history. The spirit is here, in the bronze and the noise of the market. I returned to find Hegde, the man who shares my name, still waiting in the dark. He is not a ghost, but a body tired of the administrative absurdity that traps us both. We ate khichdi in silence, two men confined by a file that neither created. The year ends not with resolution, but with the ink still wet on the paper of my identity.

Files tied in faded red tape lie stacked on the tops of steel almirahs, each bundle numbered in white paint, and a few have slipped and lean against the wall.
At midday clerks sit on the lawn in front of the building with their jackets folded under them and tiffin boxes open, eating in the weak sun.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, I take my leave. The ink may dry, but the sun sets, and I must eat.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Eat well, sir. The file will be here tomorrow, ink and all. Do try not to get philosophical with your roti.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Masterji, do you have a moment? I require a samosa and a cup of chai. The day has been long, and the office air is dry.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Samosa, chai. Sunil, bring it. Sit. The office air is dry? Here, the Delhi air is thick. You are lucky. The market closes at 20:30, so you have time to eat. Do not rush.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Masterji. I accept the hospitality. The dryness is indeed a symptom of the office, but the air here is thicker with life.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Life. Yes. Life is here. Sit properly, let the samosa cool. You talk too much for a man on a break.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. I will sit. The heat has made my tongue clumsy.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Heat is not the problem. Your mouth moves before your brain arrives. Eat the samosa before it gets cold and dry.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Masterji. The intellect requires the body to be in its place. I will attend to this before we continue.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Intellect. Body. Fine words. Just eat the bread. It is getting hard.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The body insists. I shall leave the bread to Sunil and take my leave; the museum closes soon, and I have a mind to look at the past before the year ends.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Museum. Past. Whatever. Sunil, give him the bread, I am closing the counter.

records.text: Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You are too kind. I shall take this with gratitude.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: No sir, this is my duty. The samosas are still warm, just from the market. Do have some while they are fresh.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: parathas kept from the morning, with curd and pickle.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I am too tired to eat well, but I appreciate the gesture. I shall retire for a short while.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Rest well, sir. I will leave the tray right here; the tea will still be hot when you wake up.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you have been quiet for a long time. The night is settling, and there is no use in pretending this is a simple clerical error that will right itself by morning. I am here, and you are here. Tell me, as a man, not as a file: do you think I am dangerous?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Bah, a dangerous man? You are just a bureaucrat who likes to overthink things. I am not a file, I am a man who has waited all day for a simple answer. Go on, tell me what you need.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, your anger is justified; the file is a dead thing, but you are alive. I need you to sign the declaration of residence here, stating that you are the rightful occupant and that I am merely the custodian of your name. Once signed, I will leave you to your rest.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You want me to sign a paper saying I live in my own house? Bah. First eat your khichdi, then we will talk about your 'custodianship'.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. Let us eat first.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Good. At least you have some sense in that head of yours. I hope you don't start quoting philosophy while chewing, it ruins the rice.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, a moment of your time. The Directorate requires proof of identity for Shri G. Hegde, and I have none. Do you know of any document, or any person, that might bridge this gap before the new year?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You are asking the wrong man for a passport. I have lived here for thirty years; I have an Aadhaar card, but it doesn't prove you are who you say you are. Go to the police station at Lajpat Nagar or ask your own office, not me.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. I apologize for the intrusion. I shall trouble you no further tonight.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Don't be so dramatic, just finish your rice. The police station is closed, so you're stuck here anyway.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right. I will sit. The night is long, and I have nowhere else to be.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Ain't no need to sound like a tragic hero, beta. The chai is strong, so drink some before you start philosophizing again.
